newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Abolition of EU duty free sales costly for Ireland.
newsitem.headline: Abolition of EU duty free sales costly for Ireland.

text.p: The abolition of intra-EU duty and tax-free sales would lead to higher freight and travel costs for Ireland and could damage the economy, a survey published on Wednesday said.

Ireland is now the only EU member without a landbridge linking it to Europe, therefore all foreign trade and travel is conducted by sea or air, a report published by economic consultants Tansey, Webster & Associates said.
The report said intra-EU duty and tax sales account for almost four-fifths of total tax free sales in Ireland and their abolition will lead to significantly reduced operator profitability.
This in turn will lead to higher travel and freight costs as operators try to compensate for the loss.
"Irish transport operators effectively utilise a part of the profits generated by duty and tax-free sales to subsidise customers' fares and charges," it said.
The abolition of duty and tax-free sales would remove this profit centre, making increased fares and charges inevitable, it said.
Irish exporters would face higher transportation and freight costs to European markets, passenger fares to and from Ireland would increase and tourism would be severely affected.
Intra-EU duty and tax-free sales are scheduled for abolition in June 1999 and thereafter duty and tax-free shopping will be restricted to passengers travelling between Ireland and non-EU countries.
The report estimated the loss of intra-EU duty and tax-free sales would have cost Irish airport authority, Aer Rianta, 25 million Irish Pounds ($36.6 million) in foregone profits in 1996.
Irish airline operators would have lost about 30 million and Irish ferry operators in the region of 9.0 million, it said.
Losses sustained by Irish international transport operators including ferries, airlines and airports, would exceed the benefits to the Irish exchequer.
"The Irish exchequer would benefit from higher tax revenues as the tax base would be extended though not perhaps, by as much as might initially be expected," the report said.
The consultants estimated that the extension of the Irish tax base to intra-EU tax-free sales in 1995 would have yielded the exchequer an additional 68 million in duties and VAT (Value Added Tax).

"This revenue yield is based on the unlikely assumption that intra-EU travellers would have continued to purchase the same volumes of goods ... and even at this maximum level it represents less than 0.5 percent of all 1995 tax revenues."
It warned that increases in sea and air fares would reverse the low access fares strategy on which tourism's success over the past decade has been based.
And as more than 70 percent of all Irish merchandise exports are destined for EU markets Irish exporters will be severely penalised by higher freight costs.
